analysis.one_liner: Directs federal banking regulators to tailor rules to each institution's risk and business model.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required banking regulators to ease rules for lower-risk institutions, never got a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The TAILOR Act would have required five federal financial regulators — including the consumer protection bureau — to shape every banking rule to limit compliance costs and burdens for the banks, credit unions, and other institutions being regulated, based on each institution's risk profile and business model. It would also have forced a review of all banking regulations adopted in the previous seven years, with revisions where regulators deemed them too burdensome. It never got a hearing or vote in the Financial Services Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit unions, and other regulated financial institutions would gain the most: every new rule, and every rule from the previous seven years, would have to be scaled back or tailored to minimize their compliance costs, liability risk, and examination burdens. Community banks and credit unions — whose arguments about disproportionate paperwork motivated the bill — would benefit directly, and larger banks would benefit from the same across-the-board softening. The bill's reporting requirements would also give institutions a formal route to press regulators for lighter treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Each of the five federal financial regulators — the OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, NCUA, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — would have to tailor every rule to limit compliance costs, liability risk, and other burdens based on the risk profile and business model of the institutions affected [S3].

Regulators would also have had to review every banking regulation adopted in the seven years before the bill's introduction and revise within three years any rule the tailoring standard found too burdensome [S3].

Each agency would report annually to the House Financial Services and Senate Banking Committees on the specific steps taken to lighten regulatory burdens, and agency heads would testify on those reports [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the people banking rules protect. Requiring the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and banking agencies to design rules around the burdens institutions face — and to reopen the previous seven years of rules — could weaken safeguards against unfair lending practices, unsafe bank behavior, and the kinds of failures the rules were written to prevent. When rules fail to prevent a bank failure or a predatory practice, depositors, borrowers, and taxpayers who backstop the system bear the cost.

drawbacks.text: Applying the tailoring mandate to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would require an agency whose core job is protecting consumers to weigh the burdens its rules place on the financial institutions it polices, a standard that could soften consumer-protection rules [S3].

The retroactive review of seven years of rules — reaching back to 2012, covering much of the post-crisis Dodd-Frank regulatory structure — could reopen and revise foundational banking and consumer safeguards [S3].

Requiring each rule to fit each class of institution could produce different rules for similarly situated banks, and the bill itself directs a report on exactly that differential treatment — a cost in consistency and enforceability that supporters would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For banks, the benefit is real and concrete: lower compliance costs, particularly for small institutions facing fixed regulatory overhead. The cost is diffuse and falls on consumers, who rely on banking rules for fair lending, safe institutions, and recourse against unfair practices. A less-burdensoned rule is not always a weaker rule — regulators already had some authority to tailor rules by institution size, and Congress had passed tailoring legislation the year before — but this bill would have made minimizing institutional burden a mandatory consideration for every rule, including consumer-protection rules, and would have applied it retroactively. The bill offered no independent mechanism for protecting consumers if tailoring weakened a rule.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Scott Tipton introduced the bill on January 24, 2019, with 23 original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no markup, no hearing on the bill, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
32 Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers are better off because the bill died: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and banking regulators kept their existing authority to write and enforce rules without a mandatory burden-minimization standard, and banks did not get the retroactive review of the previous seven years of regulations. Banks that wanted lighter compliance obligations are the party that lost out.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: The committee she chaired received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, hearing, or vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 32 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required regulators to limit compliance costs, liability, and examination burdens for every class of institution, and to reopen seven years of existing rules. The financial gain to institutions comes directly out of the strength of the rules that protect depositors, borrowers, and the taxpayers who backstop bank failures.

Small institutions face fixed regulatory overhead that weighs on them disproportionately, and risk-based tailoring is a fair response to that. But the same softening would also apply to larger and riskier institutions, so their interest in this bill ran partly against the consumers the rules protect.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau was explicitly covered by the bill's tailoring mandate, meaning its rules — designed to protect borrowers and account holders — would have had to be weighed against the burdens they place on the institutions being policed, with a retroactive review of existing rules.
